own_scenes.desc: Metroplex, Transmat y KMS se instalaron en el mismo edificio de Gratiot Avenue, en el Eastern Market, un rincón de la ciudad que todavía «funcionaba»: la cercanía les permitía aprender unos de otros y remezclarse. Surgió una especie de escalafón por el que los DJs jóvenes ascendían editando cinta de bobina (un truco típico del techno de Detroit es insertar un compás al revés, imitando los rewinds de los DJs), luego remezclando y programando cajas de ritmos, hasta que la tecnología se abarató. Por allí pasaron Anthony «Shake» Shakir, que se pasó a la electrónica porque el R&B de principios de los ochenta «era una mierda», y muchos otros músicos, promotores y gente de A&R que mantenían los sellos mientras sus dueños giraban.

refs.q: One signature trick used in Detroit techno is simply editing in a reversed segment or “bar” of music, mimicking DJ backspins and “rewinds.”
refs.para: As this techno scene developed, a semiformal progression emerged by which DJs would become promoted to full-fledged artists and producers. Digital recording techniques were not yet commonplace, so most recordings were put on reel-to-reel tape. Then came the time-consuming job of editing tape (a real chore before things went digital), a task that young, aspiring DJs were only too happy to perform as it meant becoming a part of the process—and sometimes even getting small credits on a label. As in spinning, tape editing requires a good ear for continuity and extreme patience. One signature trick used in Detroit techno is simply editing in a reversed segment or “bar” of music, mimicking DJ backspins and “rewinds.” From the editing stage, some DJs plunged right into buying their own equipment; others took smaller steps, moving from editing to remixing to drum programming.
